# Chapter 4 — The Shape of the Machine

::: {.callout-note}
## In this chapter
A narrative portrait of the host whose shape encodes its decisions: Windows
Server 2025 chosen for operator continuity, IIS alone facing the network,
Gitea reachable only on the loopback, relational state in PostgreSQL, and the
quietest decision of all — identity, where the same coordinate that reads the
forest authorizes the push. This is description, not procedure; the procedure
has its own home, named in the final chapter.
:::

## A Description, Not a Procedure

It helps to picture the host, because its shape encodes its decisions. This
is a description, not a procedure — the procedure has its own home, and the
final chapter points to it. What follows is the architecture as an operator
would narrate it while walking a colleague through the rack.

## The Foundation: Windows Server 2025

The foundation is Windows Server 2025, chosen not for novelty but for
continuity. The federal customer base already runs Active Directory, the
certificate authority, IIS, and Windows Server at scale, with PowerShell as
its lingua franca and AppLocker and code-integrity tooling already in hand. A
Windows-native authority inherits all of that operator competence directly,
where a Linux alternative would impose a new operational stack on a substrate
the rest of the architecture assumes is Windows-administered. The host is
domain-joined to the legacy forest and registered in the modern tenant at
once — straddling both authorities deliberately, because the estate it
governs straddles them too.

## One Door at the Edge

At the edge sits IIS, and IIS alone faces the network. It terminates TLS on
the standard secure port, sets the security headers that a hardened web
front-end is expected to set, and forwards every request inward. Behind it,
reachable only on the loopback interface, runs Gitea — the Git service
proper, with its web interface, its API, its issues and pull requests and
hook machinery. Gitea is never bound to the public interface; the only
process the outside world can reach is the reverse proxy in front of it.

> One door, watched, logging every authenticated principal on every request,
> feeding the same telemetry pipeline as everything else in the estate.

## Memory: Repositories, State, Secrets

Beneath the Git service is its memory, and where each kind of state lives is a
deliberate choice:

| State | Where it lives | Why |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Canon (bare object stores) | Dedicated data volume, scoped ACLs | The corpus itself, isolated and permissioned |
| Relational state | PostgreSQL on a separate host | Keeps the Git service stateless of its database |
| Large binary artifacts | Git LFS server, native | Weight without bloating history |
| Secrets | Managed secret store under the service identity | Never pasted into config files |

## The Quietest Decision: Identity

The most consequential decision is the quietest one. Gitea does not run as a
person and does not run as an all-powerful local account. It runs as a
group-managed service account — a machine identity the directory itself issues
and rotates, with exactly the rights it needs and no more. Operators,
meanwhile, never authenticate to the host as the host; they authenticate as
themselves. Internal staff arrive over secure LDAP against the forest, mapped
to native identities; contributors who live in the modern tenant arrive over
OpenID Connect, their group claims flowing in with them.

The effect is the one the whole series has been building toward: the same
identity that authorizes a read of the forest authorizes a push to canon.
There is no second identity bridge to maintain, no parallel account store to
drift out of sync — the coordinate the enterprise already trusts is the
coordinate that opens the door. That door, and what it checks before it
opens, is where the architecture finally pays off. The next chapter stands at
it.
